newsitem.title: INDIA: India's ailing stocks depend on foreign funds.
newsitem.headline: India's ailing stocks depend on foreign funds.

text.p: Foreign fund managers are likely to pull select Indian stocks higher this week, prompted by year-end window-dressing of their portfolios, brokers and analysts said at the weekend.
"The only thing going for this market is the year-end scramble to tidy the books," said one dealer with a foreign broking firm.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) were the main buyers on Indian bourses in 1996, and most of them have suffered losses with the benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index plummeting about 30 percent since a peak in June.
The FIIs have sold shares to lock in profits or to cut losses, but will now look to stronger closing values for their portfolio stocks, the dealer said.
The BSE top-30 index ended last week higher by 54.95 points, or 1.94 percent, from the previous week, at 2,881.15. But the underlying trend remains shaky, market players maintain.
"The Indian market is going through a gut-wrenching bear phase which looks set to end with a 10 percent downside from current levels," said Prime Broking Company in a report.

Slides in first half company earnings, slowing industrial growth, high long-term interest rates, weak political leadership and low commodity prices were some of the factors that have undermined the markets.

Analysts said sentiment also has been hurt because of an increase in government fixed prices of petrol and diesel, which was seen as inevitable due to higher world prices and rising domestic consumption.
"India has nothing to offer at the moment," said a foreign fund manager. "At best, it is a defensive buy."
He said if the U.S. market took a big hit, Indian markets could hope to get "money by default" as fund managers direct more investments to potentially promising emerging markets.
"We expect the market to stabilise in the range of 2,500-3,200 over the next three months," Prime Broking analyst Ashish Kacholia said in the report.
"The upside...is largely on account of the annual expectations of the budget and higher FII inflows in the new calendar year."
India's annual budget is traditionally presented to parliament in the last week of February.

"For long-term value investors, this market offers an excellent opportunity," Kacholia said. "We recommend that investors should gradually begin investing, leaving aside a cash buffer of about 25 percent."
